claims.text: Applying an ultrathin ceramic coating to AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA fasteners will improve resistance to surface-initiated creep.
Applying an ultrathin ceramic coating will improve the fasteners' oxidation and corrosion resistance under extreme temperature fluctuations and long-term loading.
The starting AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA has a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure.
The starting EHEA can be produced by conventional casting.
The starting EHEA has a favorable strength–ductility balance.
The starting alloy has limited resistance to surface degradation under harsh service conditions.
Aircraft and spacecraft fastener service conditions include cyclic temperatures up to approximately 700°C, prolonged loading, and corrosive exposure.
The deposition will produce a conformal, adherent ceramic coating with a coherent coating–alloy interface.
Coating deposition can leave the alloy's underlying lamellar microstructure unaltered.
The ceramic coating will act as a barrier to oxygen, moisture, and corrosive species.
The coating will mitigate surface stress concentrations that can initiate creep deformation.
Preventing surface degradation will preserve the alloy's bulk mechanical properties.
Coated fasteners will exhibit lower creep rates than uncoated fasteners.
Coated fasteners will exhibit less corrosion damage than uncoated fasteners.
The coating will extend fastener operational life.
The coating will not compromise the alloy's inherent strength and ductility.
Uncoated AlCoCrFeNi2.1 fasteners are prone to corrosion and surface-initiated creep under extreme service conditions.
Any improvement depends on the coating remaining free of cracking and delamination during thermal and mechanical cycling.
Any improvement depends on deposition not adversely altering the alloy's bulk microstructure.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the ceramic coating and alloy substrate could cause delamination or crack propagation during cyclic loading.
